title: Mixed practice: How rain happens
description: One set with every response type: reading, listening, speaking and writing about the water cycle.

stimuli.title: How Rain Happens
paragraphs: Rain does not start in the sky. It starts on the ground, in oceans, lakes, and puddles. When the sun shines on water, some of the water warms up and turns into a gas called water vapor. This change is called evaporation. The water vapor is invisible, and it rises into the air.

High above the ground, the air is much colder. When water vapor reaches the cold air, it cools down and turns back into tiny drops of water. This change is called condensation. Millions of these drops gather together, and they form a cloud.

Inside a cloud, the tiny drops bump into each other and join. They grow bigger and heavier. When the drops are too heavy to stay up, they fall to the ground as rain. Falling water is called precipitation.

The rain flows into streams and rivers, and the rivers carry the water back to the ocean. Then the sun warms the water again, and the cycle starts over. Because the water keeps moving in this way, we call it the water cycle.

stimuli.title: Listen: A plant experiment
stimuli.script: Today we will plant a bean seed. First, fill a small cup with soil. Next, push the seed into the soil with your finger, about as deep as your first knuckle. Then, add a little water. Not too much, because the seed can rot. Finally, put the cup near a sunny window. Check it every morning and write what you see.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Think about how rain forms. Explain the steps of the water cycle to a classmate who missed the lesson. Use the words first, next, then, and finally.

stimuli.title: Writing task
paragraphs: Explain how rain forms. Use details from the passage “How Rain Happens.” Tell what happens first, what happens next, and why the water falls.

items.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Oceans are bigger than lakes and rivers.
Rain begins when water on the ground warms, rises, cools, and falls again.
Clouds are made of invisible gas.
The sun is hotter in the summer.

distractors.a: The passage never compares the size of oceans, lakes, and rivers.
distractors.c: Water vapor is invisible, but the passage says clouds are made of tiny drops of water.
distractors.d: The passage talks about the sun warming water, not about seasons.

items.explanation: The whole passage follows water as it warms, rises, cools into clouds, and falls as rain.

support.clue: Ask what all four paragraphs are about together. Look at the last sentence: it names the whole process.
support.frame: The passage explains how ______ goes up, forms ______, and comes back down as ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different topic). A passage about a puddle says: “The sun warms a puddle. The water turns into vapor and rises. By afternoon the puddle is gone.” Its main idea: A puddle dries because the sun turns its water into vapor.

Now find the one sentence that tells the big idea of your passage the same way.

items.stem: Which two details explain why water vapor turns into drops?

options.text: The sun shines on the ocean.
The air high above the ground is cold.
Rivers carry water to the sea.

distractors.a: This explains evaporation, the first step, not the change into drops.
distractors.c: This happens after the rain falls.

items.explanation: Condensation happens when water vapor reaches cold air and cools down.

support.clue: Reread paragraph 2. Find the sentence that begins with “When water vapor reaches the cold air.”
support.frame: Water vapor turns into drops because it ______ and the air is ______.
support.model: Mentor example. “A cold glass of juice gets wet on the outside because warm air touches the cold glass and the vapor in the air cools down.” The cause is the cooling, not the glass being full.

items.stem: Complete the explanation with the best words.

dropdown.template: First, the sun {1} the water, so the water {2} into vapor. Later, the drops {3} together and form a cloud.

items.explanation: The sun warms the water; the water turns into vapor; the tiny drops gather together to form a cloud.

support.clue: Read paragraphs 1 and 2 slowly. Each blank is a verb that tells what happens to water.
support.frame: First the sun ______ the water. Then the water ______ into a gas.
support.model: Mentor example. “First, the baker heats the dough, so the dough turns into bread. Later, the loaves cool together on a rack.” Notice that each blank names an action in time order.

items.stem: Put the steps of the water cycle in order.

items.text: The drops grow heavy and fall as rain.
The sun warms water and it turns into vapor.
Rivers carry the water back to the ocean.
The vapor cools and forms a cloud.

support.clue: Look for words that show time in the passage: “When,” “Inside,” “Then.” Which step must happen before a cloud can form?
support.model: Mentor example for planting a seed: First, you put the seed in soil. Next, you add water. Then, a small sprout grows. Finally, leaves open. Order your steps the same way.

items.stem: Match each science word to its meaning.

right.text: water vapor turns into tiny drops
liquid water turns into a gas

items.explanation: Each word is defined in the passage right after it is named.

support.clue: Each word is named in the passage right after its meaning. Find where each word appears.
support.model: Mentor example. “Hibernation is when an animal sleeps through the winter.” The word comes after the description, and the description tells the meaning.

items.stem: Sort each sentence: is it a cause or an effect?

tokens.text: The air high above the ground is cold.
Water vapor turns into tiny drops.
The drops are too heavy to stay up.

items.explanation: The cold air causes the vapor to turn into drops; the heavy drops cause rain to fall.

support.clue: Ask “why?” for each sentence. If the sentence answers “why,” it is a cause.
support.model: Mentor example. “The ground is wet because it rained.” Rained is the cause; wet ground is the effect.

items.stem: What should students do right after they push the seed into the soil?

options.text: Put the cup near a window.

distractors.d: That happens every morning, after the plant is set up.

items.explanation: The speaker says: First soil, next the seed, then a little water.

support.clue: Listen for the signal words first, next, then, and finally. The question asks what comes after the seed.
support.frame: After the seed goes in the soil, you ______.
support.model: Mentor example. “First, wash the apple. Next, cut it. Then, put it in a bowl.” After cutting comes the bowl.

items.stem: Explain how rain forms. Use details from the passage.

checklist: I explained why the water falls.
I used at least two science words from the passage.

support.clue: Reread each paragraph and underline one event. Put the events in time order.
support.frame: First, the sun ______. Next, the water vapor ______. Then, the drops ______ and fall as rain because ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a puddle. “First, the sun shines on a puddle. Next, the water warms and turns into vapor. Then the puddle gets smaller because the vapor rises into the air.” Notice how each sentence starts with a time word and ends with a reason or result.

Write your own explanation about rain in the same way.

items.stem: Explain the steps of the water cycle.

checklist: I used first, next, then, and finally.
I named evaporation, condensation, or precipitation.
I explained why the water falls.

support.clue: Plan four short sentences, one for each step. Say the time word first.
support.model: Mentor example. “First, the sun warms the puddle. Next, the water turns into vapor. Then the vapor rises. Finally, the puddle disappears.” Say yours about rain.
